items.topic: Continuous injection/withdrawal requirement for pipeline operation
items.definition: A pipeline only functions because gas is continuously injected at the high-pressure (supply) end and continuously withdrawn at the low-pressure (consumer) end; if either side stops for economic reasons, the pressure differential collapses and the pipeline stops moving gas.
items.core_idea: Because pipeline flow depends entirely on maintaining a pressure gradient, operators may have to keep injecting and withdrawing gas even when it looks uneconomical, since restarting a stalled pipeline takes significant time.
key_points: Gas only flows from high-pressure zones to low-pressure zones
Injections and withdrawals cannot be halted purely because they are unprofitable at a given moment without risking pipeline shutdown
Restarting a pipeline after a stoppage takes time, so it may need to keep running even with no active consumer demand and no available storage
relationships: Compressor stations maintain this pressure differential
Explains why pipeline operators rely on interruptible customers to keep pressure up
trading_implications: Pipeline operators have structural reasons to keep moving gas regardless of short-term economics, which affects how reliably interruptible capacity is offered
common_misunderstandings: Assuming pipeline flow can be freely started and stopped like a valve, without consequence for the broader network

items.definition: Mechanical facilities spaced along a pipeline that create the pressure differentials needed to push gas forward, functioning like a heart pumping blood through the network.
items.core_idea: A compressor station works like a household fan: it draws gas in on a low-pressure side and discharges it on a high-pressure side, and chaining many such stations together in series keeps gas flowing continuously down the pipeline.
key_points: Simple mental model: a fan pulls gas in (low pressure zone) on one side and pushes it out (high pressure zone) on the other
Stations are typically spaced roughly every 50 miles along a pipeline
A modern station usually runs several compressor units in parallel
Gas path through a station: suction header, then a scrubber system, then compression/cooling stages, then discharge into the next pipeline segment
Gas moves between segments by flowing from one station's high-pressure discharge to the next station's low-pressure suction
All stations on a pipeline must operate in coordination or the whole pipeline stops working; most are automated and coordinated by a central computer
relationships: Depends on the continuous injection/withdrawal requirement
Cooling stages tie into compression heating/corrosion effects
trading_implications: Physical pipeline capacity is not a single uniform pipe but a chain of segments bounded by compressor stations, which is relevant to understanding where physical constraints or outages could occur
common_misunderstandings: Thinking of a pipeline as one continuous unregulated pipe rather than a series of pressure-managed segments

items.topic: Compression heating, cooling, and impurity removal
items.definition: Compressing gas raises its temperature; since cold gas is denser than hot gas, cooling the gas after compression lets more gas mass be moved at a given pipeline pressure, and also reduces corrosion caused by trace impurities.
items.core_idea: Compressor stations cool gas after compression both to increase the effective transport capacity of the pipeline and to limit corrosion from the trace non-methane gases that are always present in natural gas.
key_points: Compression inherently increases gas temperature
Colder gas is denser, so at a constant operating pressure more gas can be transported if it is kept cool
Cooler gas causes less corrosion in the pipeline
Natural gas is never pure methane and always carries trace amounts of other gases, some of which are corrosive
Compressor stations include scrubbing systems to remove these trace impurities and particulates/liquids before compression, preventing mechanical breakdowns
relationships: Part of the compressor station process described above
common_misunderstandings: Assuming compression is a purely mechanical pressure-boosting step with no thermal or gas-quality side effects

items.definition: Firm service guarantees pipeline capacity availability except for force majeure events and costs a premium; interruptible service is cheaper, offered on a best-efforts basis, and can be curtailed for valid operational reasons, most commonly to keep the pipeline's pressure balanced.
items.core_idea: Shippers trade off cost against reliability: firm service buys guaranteed capacity via a reservation charge, while interruptible service is cheap but can be shut off whenever the pipeline operator needs to balance flow or serve a firm shipper's actual delivery.
key_points: Firm service: guaranteed except for force majeure; relatively expensive
Interruptible service: best-efforts basis, relatively cheap, can be interrupted for any valid reason, most commonly pipeline balancing
A firm shipper pays a reservation charge to guarantee available capacity but is not obligated to actually inject gas into the pipeline

When a firm shipper isn't using its reserved capacity (e.g., an unusually warm winter reducing heating demand), the pipeline operator sells cheaper interruptible service to other parties to keep the line pressurized
When the firm shipper does want to deliver, interruptible customers are shut off first
Public utilities delivering residential heat, and power plants/industrial facilities, tend to prefer firm service for reliability
Storage facilities may prefer interruptible service because they want to buy gas cheaply during low-demand periods, which is exactly when interruptible contracts tend to be active
relationships: Builds on the pipeline continuity requirement
trading_implications: Storage operators can use interruptible contracts to buy gas cheaply during low-demand windows without paying the firm-service reliability premium
Knowing which counterparties hold firm vs. interruptible contracts helps anticipate whose gas flows get curtailed first when the pipeline needs to balance
common_misunderstandings: Assuming interruptible service is simply a discount version of firm service rather than a fundamentally lower-priority, curtailable claim on capacity
related_topics: Gas commingling and pipeline fullness economics

items.topic: Gas commingling and pipeline fullness economics
items.definition: Gas injected into a pipeline mixes with the gas already there and moves according to pressure gradients rather than as a discrete tracked parcel, so the molecules withdrawn at a delivery point are not literally the same molecules injected upstream; how well injected volumes can be matched by withdrawals elsewhere depends heavily on how full the pipeline already is.
items.core_idea: Pipeline 'transportation' is really a displacement process: in a nearly full pipeline, injecting gas at one point and withdrawing roughly the same volume elsewhere can happen almost immediately, but in a nearly empty pipeline the injected gas spreads throughout the line and cannot practically be fully recovered at the intended delivery point.
key_points: The rate gas flows depends on the pressure difference between two points; higher-pressure gas moves faster
In a multi-segment pipeline, gas injected at one point disperses across the system rather than traveling as a discrete unit to a specific exit
If the pipeline is already nearly full, simultaneous injection and withdrawal at different points can approximate near-instant transportation because the system is close to equilibrium
If the pipeline starts nearly empty, injected gas spreads throughout its length, making it practically impossible to withdraw the full injected quantity at the intended point
Pipeline operators therefore have a strong incentive to keep pipelines nearly full, though not at true maximum capacity (which would prevent further injection) and not at very low pressure either
relationships: Explains why pipeline operators need interruptible buyers/sellers to manage fullness
trading_implications: Gas nominated for delivery at a specific point is a claim on volume, not on specific molecules, which is part of why pipeline balancing and fullness management matter operationally
common_misunderstandings: Assuming pipeline transportation moves a specific parcel of gas directly from injection point to withdrawal point, like cargo on a train

items.definition: A tariff is the publicly filed fee schedule a regulated pipeline charges for its services, obtainable from either the pipeline company or its regulating agency.
items.core_idea: Nearly every pipeline available for public use in the U.S. is regulated and required to publish its charges in a public tariff document.
key_points: Applies to regulated pipelines, which covers essentially all pipelines available for public use in the U.S.
Tariffs can be obtained from the pipeline company or the regulating agency
relationships: Contains charges such as the Annual Cost Adjustment

items.definition: The ACA is a small tariff charge added to pipeline transportation costs to adjust for inflation.
items.core_idea: A minor, inflation-linked line-item fee within a pipeline's published tariff.
key_points: Adjusts transportation costs for inflation
relationships: Listed as part of a pipeline's tariff
